title: The Federation Army on Paper: How Far Zagreb Would Let Go
sources: ICTY Prlic et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T)
Balkan Battlegrounds (CIA Office of Russian and European Analysis, 2002), Vol. II
content:
The Washington Agreement of March 1994 created, on paper, a Federation Army charged to absorb the HVO and the ARBiH into a single unified military structure. Six months on, the paper architecture had not bitten. HVO brigades in central Bosnia, Mostar, and western Herzegovina held Federation Army table-of-organization slots in name, but they answered in practice through the Mostar Defence Department and the Zagreb-Susak channel — not through the Federation general staff.

The question recorded on the Croat side was how far Zagreb would let go. Integration meant subordinating Croat formations to a joint command in which Bosniak officers would hold a share of authority proportionate to the larger ARBiH. For a leadership that had fought a year-long war to establish a separate Croat military space, full integration was a profound concession — and Tudjman’s government, as the patron that supplied and sustained the HVO, held an effective veto over how completely it occurred.

The documented historical posture was parallel commands: the status quo. ICRC and UNPROFOR field reports across the former front recorded persistent dual command structures through the Vienna framework of March 1994, the Contact Group process of July, and on through Dayton at the end of 1995. The Tudjman-Susak correspondence admitted in the ICTY Prlic et al. proceedings records Zagreb’s preference for the HVO retaining a parallel Croat command line inside the Federation’s paper architecture. Operational integration was nominal, not substantive.

The alternatives would each have meant a different degree of letting go. Full integration would have merged the HVO and ARBiH into a genuine Federation Army with a unified staff. Selective integration would have shared a joint staff while keeping troops under separate national chains. Refusing integration outright would have rejected even the paper structure. The historical leadership chose the option that satisfied the agreement’s form while preserving the substance of a separate Croat command — parallel commands behind a Federation facade.

The gap between the paper army and the real one was a deliberate construction. It allowed Herceg-Bosna to claim compliance with the Federation while retaining the military autonomy that the Susak channel underwrote. That gap persisted until Dayton, and its persistence is the clearest measure of how far Zagreb was, in the end, willing to let go: far enough to sign, not far enough to merge.
